name: Aspect-scaled width
description: Finds the new width that preserves the original aspect ratio for a given new height, using new height × original width / original height.
notes: Keeps the image proportions unchanged so it is not distorted. Round to whole pixels as needed; the same ratio logic applies when scaling by width instead.

name: Aspect ratio height
description: Computes the height that matches a target aspect ratio for a given width, using width × ratio height / ratio width (for example 16:9).
notes: Ratio height and width are the ratio terms (e.g. 9 and 16), not pixel sizes. Result may need rounding to whole pixels.

name: Photo print scaling
description: Scales a photo or print dimension by a percentage using original size × scale / 100. A scale over 100 enlarges and under 100 shrinks the size.
notes: Enter the scale as a percentage (150 means 150%). Apply the same scale to both width and height to keep proportions.

name: Exposure Value (EV)
description: Computes the photographic exposure value from the f-number and shutter time as the base-2 logarithm of N² divided by t. Each whole EV step represents a doubling or halving of the exposure.
notes: This is EV at ISO 100; other sensitivities shift the value. Shutter time is in seconds, so a 1/100 s exposure is entered as 0.01, and larger f-numbers or shorter times raise EV.

name: Elo Rating Update
description: Updates a competitor's Elo rating after a match by adding the K-factor times the difference between the actual score (1 win, 0.5 draw, 0 loss) and the expected score. Beating expectations raises the rating; underperforming lowers it.
notes: The expected score Es must come from the two players' ratings and lie between 0 and 1. A larger K-factor makes ratings move faster but noisier.

name: Elo Expected Score
description: Gives a player's expected score (win probability, counting draws as half) against an opponent from their rating difference, using the logistic Elo curve with a 400-point scale. Equal ratings give 0.5; a 400-point edge gives about 0.909.
notes: Result is a probability between 0 and 1, not a percentage times 100. The 400 scaling and base-10 form are the standard chess Elo convention.

name: Equal Temperament Frequency
description: Gives the frequency in hertz of a pitch a given number of semitones from A4, as 440 times 2 to the power of semitones over 12. Each semitone multiplies frequency by the twelfth root of 2 in equal temperament.
notes: The semitone count is signed: positive goes up, negative goes down from A4. It assumes A4 = 440 Hz and 12-tone equal temperament, not just intonation.

name: Interval in Cents
description: Measures a musical interval in cents from the ratio of two frequencies, as 1200 times the base-2 logarithm of the ratio. One octave is 1200 cents and one equal-tempered semitone is 100 cents.
notes: Enter the upper frequency over the lower so the result is positive; equal frequencies give 0 cents. The measure is logarithmic, so equal cents mean equal perceived interval size.

name: Frequency Ratio from Cents
description: Converts an interval size in cents into a frequency ratio, as 2 raised to the power of cents over 1200. It is the inverse of the cents formula, turning a logarithmic interval back into a multiplicative frequency factor.
notes: Result is a dimensionless ratio to multiply a base frequency by; 1200 cents gives exactly 2. Negative cents yield a ratio below 1, lowering the pitch.

name: Mersenne's Law (String Frequency)
description: Computes the fundamental frequency in hertz of a vibrating string from its length, tension, and linear mass density, as one over twice the length times the square root of tension over density. Higher tension raises pitch; greater length or mass lowers it.
notes: Use SI units: length in meters, tension in newtons, density in kg/m. It gives the fundamental only for an ideal flexible string, ignoring stiffness and overtones.

name: Open Pipe Fundamental Frequency
description: Gives the fundamental frequency in hertz of a pipe open at both ends, as the speed of sound divided by twice the pipe length. Such a pipe supports a full wavelength of twice its length at the fundamental.
notes: Applies to pipes open at both ends, which produce all harmonics. It omits the end correction, so real pipes sound slightly lower than predicted.

name: Closed Pipe Fundamental Frequency
description: Gives the fundamental frequency in hertz of a pipe closed at one end, as the speed of sound divided by four times the pipe length. A closed pipe fits a quarter wavelength, sounding an octave lower than an open pipe of equal length.
notes: Applies to pipes closed at one end, which produce only odd harmonics. It omits the end correction, so real instruments sound slightly lower.

name: Pipe Frequency with End Correction
description: Computes an open pipe's fundamental frequency in hertz including an end correction, dividing the speed of sound by twice the effective length, where the effective length adds 0.6 times the diameter. This corrects for air vibrating just beyond the open end.
notes: All lengths must be in the same unit. The 0.6d term approximates the combined correction for both open ends (about 0.3d each); the constant varies with flanging, and wide pipes need a larger correction.

name: nth Harmonic Frequency
description: Gives the frequency in hertz of the nth harmonic of a tone, as the harmonic number times the fundamental frequency. The harmonics form the integer-multiple series that shapes an instrument's timbre.
notes: Here n=1 is the fundamental itself, so the nth harmonic is the (n-1)th overtone. This assumes an ideal harmonic series; real strings and pipes are slightly inharmonic.

name: Beat Period from BPM
description: Converts a tempo in beats per minute to the duration of one beat in milliseconds, as 60000 divided by the BPM. It answers how many milliseconds each beat lasts at a given tempo.
notes: Output is milliseconds because 60000 is 60 seconds in ms; use 60 instead for seconds. One beat here means one quarter note in common time.

name: Note Duration from Tempo
description: Gives the duration in milliseconds of a note of a given value at a set tempo, as 240000 divided by BPM times the note value, where 4 is a quarter note and 8 an eighth. Larger note values give shorter durations.
notes: The note value follows the fraction convention (4=quarter, 8=eighth, 16=sixteenth). Output is milliseconds and assumes the beat is a quarter note.

name: Tempo-Synced Delay Time
description: Computes a tempo-synced delay time in milliseconds, as 60000 divided by BPM times the number of subdivisions per beat. Higher subdivision counts give shorter echoes that lock to the musical grid.
notes: Subdivisions per beat set the rhythmic value: 1 is a quarter, 2 an eighth, 4 a sixteenth. Output is milliseconds; use dotted or triplet factors for those feels.

name: Speed of Sound from Temperature
description: Estimates the speed of sound in air in m/s from temperature, as 331.3 times the square root of one plus temperature in Celsius over 273.15. Sound travels faster as air warms.
notes: Temperature must be in degrees Celsius; the formula converts to absolute temperature internally. It is for dry air at standard pressure and ignores humidity effects.

name: Wavelength of a Pitch
description: Gives the wavelength in meters of a sound of a given frequency, as the speed of sound divided by frequency. Lower pitches have longer wavelengths, which matters for room modes and speaker placement.
notes: Use a speed of sound matching the actual air temperature for accuracy. Frequency in hertz and speed in m/s give wavelength in meters.

name: String Tension for Target Pitch
description: Computes the tension in newtons a string needs to sound a target pitch, as the linear mass density times the square of twice the length times the frequency. It inverts Mersenne's law to solve for the required tension.
notes: Use SI units: density in kg/m, length in meters, frequency in hertz. It gives the fundamental-mode tension for an ideal string and ignores stiffness.

name: Fret Position on a String
description: Gives the distance in meters from the nut to the nth fret, as the scale length times one minus 2 to the power of minus n over 12. Frets follow the twelfth-root-of-2 spacing of equal temperament, crowding together toward the bridge.
notes: Distance is measured from the nut, not the bridge, and shares units with scale length. It assumes ideal equal temperament and no compensation for string stiffness or intonation.

name: Phons from Sones
description: Converts loudness in sones to loudness level in phons, as 40 plus 10 times the base-2 logarithm of the sone value. Each doubling of sones adds 10 phons, because the sone scale is defined so that a 10-phon rise doubles perceived loudness.
notes: Valid above 1 sone (40 phons), where the doubling relationship holds; below that the scale bends. Phons equal decibels only at 1 kHz on equal-loudness contours.

name: Sones from Phons
description: Converts a loudness level in phons to loudness in sones, as 2 to the power of phons minus 40 over 10. It inverts the sone-phon relation so that every 10-phon rise doubles the sone value and the perceived loudness.
notes: Reference point is 1 sone at 40 phons. The formula holds above 40 phons; below that perceived loudness falls off faster than it predicts.

name: Eyring Reverberation Time
description: Estimates reverberation time RT60 in seconds using the Eyring equation, from room volume, total surface area, and the mean absorption coefficient. It predicts how long sound takes to decay by 60 dB, and stays valid in rooms with high absorption.
notes: The mean absorption coefficient is a fraction between 0 and 1; the logarithm term makes it more accurate than Sabine's formula when absorption is large. The 0.161 constant assumes SI units.

name: Critical Distance (Room Acoustics)
description: Estimates the critical distance in meters from a sound source, where the direct and reverberant sound fields are equal, as 0.057 times the square root of room volume over reverberation time. Beyond it, reverberant sound dominates.
notes: Volume is in cubic meters and RT60 in seconds; the 0.057 constant assumes an omnidirectional source in SI units. Directional sources shift the true critical distance.

name: Doppler-Shifted Pitch
description: Computes the frequency in hertz heard from a source moving toward a stationary listener, as the source frequency times the speed of sound over the speed of sound minus the source speed. Approaching motion raises the pitch.
notes: This form assumes the listener is at rest and the source moves toward them; a receding source needs a sign change on vs. Source speed must stay below the speed of sound.

name: MIDI Note Number to Frequency
description: Converts a MIDI note number to its frequency in hertz, as 440 times 2 to the power of the note number minus 69 over 12. Note 69 is A4 at 440 Hz, and each step of one adds a semitone.
notes: Assumes A4 = 440 Hz and 12-tone equal temperament; MIDI 69 is the reference. Middle C is note 60, though some software labels it C3 versus C4.

name: Frequency to MIDI Note Number
description: Converts a frequency in hertz to a MIDI note number, as 69 plus 12 times the base-2 logarithm of the frequency over 440. It inverts the MIDI-to-frequency map, returning A4 = 69 and adding 12 per octave.
notes: Result is generally non-integer; round to the nearest whole number for the closest note and read the fraction as cents of detuning. Assumes A4 = 440 Hz.

name: Sound Pressure Level Ratio (dB)
description: Gives the level difference in decibels between two sound pressures, as 20 times the base-10 logarithm of their ratio. The factor of 20 applies because sound intensity scales with pressure squared.
notes: Both pressures use the same unit since only their ratio matters; enter the reference as p1. A pressure ratio of 10 equals 20 dB, and doubling the pressure is about 6 dB.

name: Frequency After n Octaves
description: Computes the frequency reached after shifting a base frequency f0 up by a given number of octaves. Each octave doubles the pitch, so the result is f0 multiplied by 2 raised to the octave count.
notes: The octave count need not be an integer; fractional values give intermediate pitches. Use a negative count to shift down. Base frequency and result share the same unit (Hz).

name: Exposure Value at ISO
description: Calculates the exposure value at a given ISO from the aperture (f-number N) and shutter time t. The first term log2(N^2/t) is EV at ISO 100, and log2(iso/100) shifts it for the actual sensitivity.
notes: Shutter time t is in seconds. EV increases by 1 for each halving of light (one stop). Higher ISO lowers the required EV, so the term is subtracted.

name: Near Limit of Depth of Field
description: Gives the nearest distance in sharp focus (the near limit of the depth of field) from the hyperfocal distance H, the focused subject distance s, and the focal length f. Everything from this distance back to the far limit appears acceptably sharp.
notes: All lengths must use the same unit; here f is in metres like H and s. H itself depends on aperture and circle of confusion, computed separately.

name: Far Limit of Depth of Field
description: Gives the farthest distance in sharp focus (the far limit of the depth of field) from the hyperfocal distance H, the focused subject distance s, and the focal length f. The scene stays acceptably sharp from the near limit out to this distance.
notes: When the subject distance equals or exceeds the hyperfocal distance, the denominator reaches zero or turns negative, meaning the far limit is at infinity. Keep all lengths in the same unit.

name: Depth of Field (Approximate)
description: Estimates the total depth of field using the approximation 2·s²·N·c/f², valid when the subject distance s is well short of the hyperfocal distance. Depth grows with subject distance squared and aperture number, and shrinks with focal length squared.
notes: This is a small-distance approximation and overestimates near the hyperfocal distance. Circle of confusion c and focal length f use the same length unit as s (metres here).

name: Aperture Diameter (Entrance Pupil)
description: Calculates the effective aperture diameter (entrance pupil) as focal length f divided by the f-number N. This is the physical light-gathering opening the f-number represents for a given focal length.
notes: The f-number is defined as f divided by this diameter, so smaller N gives a larger opening. Result shares the focal length unit (mm here).

name: Angle of View
description: Gives the angle of view in degrees for a sensor dimension d and focal length f, using 2·atan(d/(2f)) converted from radians. It describes how wide a scene the lens captures along that sensor edge or diagonal.
notes: Sensor dimension and focal length must share a unit (mm). Choose d as width, height, or diagonal to get the corresponding horizontal, vertical, or diagonal angle. This is a thin-lens approximation ignoring focus distance.

name: 35mm-Equivalent Focal Length
description: Converts an actual lens focal length to its 35mm-equivalent by multiplying by the sensor crop factor. This gives the focal length a full-frame camera would need for the same angle of view.
notes: The crop factor is the ratio of the full-frame diagonal to the sensor diagonal (about 1.5 for APS-C, 2 for Micro Four Thirds). Result keeps the input length unit (mm).

name: Crop Factor from Sensor Diagonal
description: Computes the crop factor by dividing the full-frame (35mm) sensor diagonal of 43.27 mm by the given sensor diagonal. The result shows how much a smaller sensor multiplies effective focal length relative to full frame.
notes: Sensor diagonal must be entered in millimetres for the 43.27 constant to apply. A diagonal equal to 43.27 mm gives a crop factor of 1 (full frame).

name: Guide Number (Flash)
description: Calculates a flash guide number as the product of the f-number N and the flash-to-subject distance dist. The guide number summarises a flash unit's power for correct exposure at a reference ISO.
notes: The guide number carries the distance unit (metres here) and is tied to a specific ISO, usually 100. Compare only guide numbers stated for the same ISO and distance unit.

name: Flash Range from Guide Number
description: Finds the maximum flash-to-subject distance for correct exposure by dividing the guide number GN by the chosen f-number N. Opening the aperture (smaller N) extends the usable flash range.
notes: The result is in the distance unit the guide number was defined with (metres here) and assumes the guide number's reference ISO. Real range also depends on subject reflectance.

name: Guide Number ISO Scaling
description: Rescales a flash guide number from a reference ISO to a target ISO by multiplying by the square root of the ISO ratio. Doubling ISO increases the guide number by a factor of about 1.41.
notes: Only the ISO ratio matters, so both ISO values may use any consistent scale. The scaled guide number keeps the distance unit of the original.

name: Handheld Shutter Speed Limit
description: Estimates the slowest handheld shutter time before camera shake blurs the image, as the reciprocal of the 35mm-equivalent focal length (focal length f times crop factor). Longer lenses demand faster shutter speeds.
notes: This is the classic 1/focal-length rule using effective focal length; the numeric result is a shutter time in seconds. Image stabilisation allows slower speeds than this guideline suggests.

name: Sunny 16 Shutter Speed
description: Gives the shutter time for the Sunny 16 rule as the reciprocal of the ISO speed, the correct exposure in bright sunlight at aperture f/16. For ISO 100 this yields about 1/100 s.
notes: Valid only at aperture f/16 in direct front sunlight; other apertures or lighting need adjustment. The result is a shutter time in seconds.

name: Field of View Width (Subject)
description: Calculates the real-world width covered at the subject plane from the subject distance, sensor width, and focal length, using dist·sensor/f. It tells how wide a scene fits in frame at that distance.
notes: Subject distance is in metres while sensor width and focal length are in millimetres; the ratio sensor/f is dimensionless, so the result comes out in the distance unit (metres). Thin-lens approximation.

name: Optical Magnification (Object Distance)
description: Computes the optical magnification of a thin lens from focal length f and object distance s, as f/(s−f). The value is the ratio of image size to object size.
notes: Object distance must exceed the focal length for a real, focused image; s equal to f gives infinite magnification. Focal length and object distance use the same unit, and the result is dimensionless.

name: Effective f-number (Macro)
description: Gives the effective f-number in close-up work as the marked f-number N multiplied by (1 + magnification m). Lens extension for macro focusing raises the effective f-number and reduces the light reaching the sensor.
notes: At 1:1 magnification (m = 1) the effective f-number doubles, a two-stop light loss. This applies to unit-focusing lenses; internal-focus designs differ.

name: Bellows Extension Factor
description: Computes the exposure correction factor for lens extension in close-up work as (1 + magnification m)². Exposure must be multiplied by this factor, or extended by its log base 2 in stops, to compensate for light loss.
notes: At 1:1 magnification the factor is 4, meaning two stops of extra exposure. This assumes a lens that focuses by extension; the result is a dimensionless multiplier.

name: Circle of Confusion (Zeiss Formula)
description: Estimates the acceptable circle of confusion for a sensor using the Zeiss formula, sensor diagonal divided by 1730. This sets the blur-spot threshold used in depth-of-field and hyperfocal calculations.
notes: Sensor diagonal is in millimetres, so the circle of confusion comes out in millimetres. The divisor 1730 reflects a standard viewing and enlargement assumption; other conventions use different values.

name: Airy Disk Diameter (Diffraction)
description: Calculates the diameter of the Airy disk from wavelength lambda and f-number N, as 2.44·lambda·N. This diffraction-limited spot size sets the smallest resolvable detail at a given aperture.
notes: Wavelength and result share the same unit (mm here). When the Airy disk exceeds the circle of confusion or pixel pitch, stopping down further softens the image (diffraction limiting).

name: Diffraction Cutoff Frequency
description: Gives the diffraction cutoff spatial frequency as the reciprocal of wavelength times f-number, 1/(lambda·N). Above this frequency a diffraction-limited lens transmits no contrast.
notes: With wavelength in millimetres the result is in line pairs per millimetre. Stopping down (larger N) lowers the cutoff, reducing the finest resolvable detail.

name: Equivalent Shutter Speed (Aperture Change)
description: Finds the shutter time that keeps exposure constant after changing the aperture, scaling the original time t1 by (N2/N1)². Since light falls with the square of the f-number, closing down requires a proportionally longer exposure.
notes: This holds exposure fixed at unchanged ISO; it does not account for reciprocity failure at very long times. Result is a shutter time in the same unit as t1 (seconds).

name: Equivalent ISO (Exposure Match)
description: Computes the ISO needed to match a reference exposure after changing both aperture and shutter time, scaling ISO1 by (N2/N1)² and by t1/t2. It keeps overall brightness constant across the new settings.
notes: Both aperture ratio and shutter ratio are dimensionless, so any consistent units work. Closing the aperture or shortening the shutter raises the required ISO.

name: EV from Scene Luminance
description: Derives the exposure value from scene luminance L and ISO speed using log2(L·iso/12.5), where 12.5 is the standard reflected-light meter calibration constant. Brighter scenes and higher ISO both raise the EV.
notes: Luminance must be in candela per square metre for the 12.5 constant to apply. This EV is referenced to ISO 100 scaling via the ISO term; the 12.5 value follows common metering standards.

name: Stops Between Two f-numbers
description: Computes the exposure difference in stops between two apertures as 2·log2(N2/N1). Because light scales with the inverse square of the f-number, each doubling of N2/N1 corresponds to two stops.
notes: A positive result means N2 is the smaller aperture (less light); a negative result means more light. The f-numbers are dimensionless, so only their ratio matters.

name: Pixel Pitch
description: Calculates the pixel pitch as the sensor width (in mm, converted to micrometres via ×1000) divided by the horizontal pixel count. It is the centre-to-centre spacing of adjacent photosites.
notes: Sensor width is entered in millimetres and the result is in micrometres. This assumes square pixels evenly spanning the sensor width, without gaps or non-imaging borders.
